ex-103-1.title: Energy transferred
ex-103-1.question:
A 1.5-kW electric kettle is used to heat some tap water.

(a) How long does it take to transfer 600 kJ of energy to the water?

(b) If another electric kettle with a higher power is used to heat the same amount of tap water, how will the answer to (a) change? Explain briefly.
ex-103-1.answer:
(a) By P = Qt ,

t = QP = 600 0001500 = 400 s

It takes 400 s.

(b) The answer to (a) will become smaller. According to Q = Pt, using a

greater power P to transfer the same amount of energy Q requires less time t.

ex-103-2.title: Heat capacity of water of different masses
ex-103-2.question:
The temperature of a glass of water rises from 15 °C to 20 °C when 4 kJ of energy is supplied to it. If the water in an entire swimming pool is heated to get the same temperature change, 5 × 1010 J of energy is required.

(a) What are the heat capacities of the two bodies?

(b) Suppose 4 kJ of energy is supplied to the glass of water. What is its final temperature if its initial temperature is 27 °C?
ex-103-2.answer:
(a) For the glass of water,

C = QΔT = 400020 – 15 = 800 J °C−1

For the pool of water,

C = QΔT = 5 × 10105 = 1 × 1010 J °C−1

(b) Final temperature = 27 + 5 = 32 °C
ex-103-2.tips:
Tip

C of the glass of water is constant. According to Q = CΔT, the same Q always gives the same ΔT.
ex-103-2.think: Why are the heat capacities of the glass of water and the pool of water different?
ex-103-2.thinkAnswer: Heat capacity is C=mc. The water has the same specific heat capacity c, but the pool contains a much greater mass m. It therefore needs more energy for the same temperature rise and has a greater heat capacity.

ex-103-3.title: Energy needed to raise temperature
ex-103-3.question:
The aluminium pot as shown below is heated. Its mass is 2 kg. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J kg−1 °C−1.

(a) Calculate the energy required to raise its temperature from 10 °C to 30 °C.

(b) Find the heat capacity of the pot.
ex-103-3.answer:
(a) Energy required = mcΔT = 2 × 900 × (30 − 10) = 36 000 J

(b) Heat capacity of the pot = mc = 2 × 900 = 1800 J °C−1

ex-103-4.title: Measuring the specific heat capacity of water
ex-103-4.question:
In Experiment 3c, the following results were obtained:

Mass of water = 0.2 kg

Initial joulemeter reading = 0

Initial temperature = 20 °C

Final joulemeter reading = 15 000 J

Final temperature = 37 °C

(a) Write the equation used to calculate the specific heat capacity of water in the experiment.

(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of water using the above data.

(c) The standard value of the specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg−1 °C−1. Find the percentage error of the result in (b).

(d) State two possible sources of error.

(e) How could you improve the accuracy of the experiment?
ex-103-4.answer:
(a) c = QmΔT

(b) Specific heat capacity of water = QmΔT = 15 0000.2 × (37 – 20) = 4410 J kg−1 °C−1

(c) Percentage error = 4410 – 42004200 × 100% = 5%

(d) Some energy is lost to the surrounding air.

Some energy is absorbed by the cup, the stirrer and the thermometer.

(e) Wrap the polystyrene cup with cotton wool to reduce energy loss to the surroundings.
ex-103-4.tips:
Skill

Mathematics

Significant figures and rounding Depending on the accuracy required, we can round the calculation result to different significant figures (sig. fig.).

Typically, answers are expressed in 3 significant figures in this series of books. p.193

Skill

Experiment

Percentage error All measurements contain errors. If the measured value of a quantity is M while the standard value of this quantity is S, the error E in this measurement is the difference between M and S, i.e. E = |M – S|. Then,

percentage error

= |M – S|S × 100%

The smaller the percentage error, the more precise the measurement.

ex-103-5.title: Final temperature of a mixture
ex-103-5.question:
Water of mass 0.5 kg at 90 °C is added to water of mass 0.2 kg at 15 °C.

(a) Estimate the final temperature T of the mixture. Take the specific heat capacity of water to be 4200 J kg−1 °C−1.

(b) The final temperature is measured to be 65 °C. Compare this value to your answer in (a) and explain the difference.
ex-103-5.answer:
(a) Energy lost by hotter water = energy gained by cooler water

0.5 × 4200 × (90 − T) = 0.2 × 4200 × (T − 15)

0.5 × (90 − T) = 0.2 × (T − 15)

T = 68.6 °C

(b) The value is lower than the answer in (a). This is because some energy is lost to the surroundings.
ex-103-5.tips:
Tip

Drawing a simple diagram may help you see the energy change in the process more easily. The red arrow represents the energy gained by the cooler water and the blue arrow represents the energy lost by the hotter water.

ex-103-6.title: Estimating the specific heat capacity of copper
ex-103-6.question:
Jim performs Experiment 3f. After the hot copper block is transferred to the water in the polystyrene cup, he measures the water temperature every minute and obtains the graph as shown.

(a) Explain the increase in water temperature from 22.7 °C to 26.7 °C in the graph.

(b) Why does the water temperature no longer rise after reaching 26.7 °C?

(c) The mass of the copper block and the water are 132 g and 200 g respectively. By taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg−1 °C−1, calculate the specific heat capacity c of copper.

(d) State one possible source of error. Explain how this error affects the value of c obtained in (c).
ex-103-6.answer:
(a) The copper block has a higher temperature than the water in the cup. Energy is transferred from the block to the water, causing the water temperature to rise.

(b) When the temperature reaches 26.7 °C, the water and the block are in thermal equilibrium.

(c) Energy lost by copper block = energy gained by water

0.132 × c × (100 − 26.7) = 0.2 × 4200 × (26.7 − 22.7)

c = 347 J kg−1 °C−1

(d) Some energy is lost to the surroundings after the copper block is transferred to the water in the cup. The highest temperature T reached by the water is lower than it should be.

As c = 0.2 × 4200 × (T – 22.7)0.132 × (100 – T), the calculated value of c becomes lower

than the actual value.
ex-103-6.tips:
Tip

Simple diagram:

Tip

A lower T would result in a lower value of (T − 22.7) and a higher value of (100 − T). Both would cause c to become lower in value.
ex-103-6.think:
1 Energy is also lost to the surroundings when the beaker of water is heated. Is this a source of error to the experiment?

2 Why does the water temperature drop after reaching the maximum value?
ex-103-6.thinkAnswer:
1 No, provided the copper block is left in boiling water long enough to reach 100 °C before transfer. Heat loss during this initial heating increases the energy and time needed, but does not change the assumed initial temperature of the block. Heat loss during transfer or mixing is a source of error.

2 At the maximum temperature, the block and water have approximately reached thermal equilibrium. They are warmer than the surroundings and continue to lose energy to them, so their temperature subsequently falls.

ex-103-7.title: Heating with a fixed power
ex-103-7.question: A 2200-W kettle heats 1.5 kg of water for two minutes. The initial temperature of the water is 25 °C. Find the final temperature T of the water if 10% of the energy is lost to the surroundings. Take the specific heat capacity of water to be 4200 J kg−1 °C−1.
ex-103-7.answer:
Energy supplied by kettle × (1 − 10%) = energy gained by water

Pt × (1 − 10%) = mcΔT

2200 × (2 × 60) × 0.9 = 1.5 × 4200 × (T − 25)

T = 62.7 °C
